--- title: "Where the Earth Shakes: Earthquakes Around the World Since 1900" description: "Earthquakes in the USGS catalogue: where in the world they strike, how often and how strong, how deep, the deadliest, and whether there are more of them than there used to be." author: "" date: "27 November 2026" --- ## What is this? An earthquake comes without warning, and the strongest can wreck a city in a minute. This story asks where they strike, and four more questions: 1. **Where in the world do the earthquakes strike?** 2. **How often, and how strong?** 3. **How deep are they?** 4. **Which were the deadliest?** 5. **Are there more of them than there used to be?** For the other hazards of the series, see [Tsunamis](ILLUSTRATION_WORLD_TSUNAMIS.html), [Volcanoes](ILLUSTRATION_WORLD_VOLCANOES.html) and the [overview of natural disasters](ILLUSTRATION_NATURAL_DISASTERS.html). The data come from three places, downloaded when the page is rendered: - **The earthquakes**: the catalogue of the **United States Geological Survey** (USGS), called ComCat, which collects the earthquakes that seismic networks around the world report: the date, the place, the magnitude and the depth ([ComCat](https://earthquake.usgs.gov/data/comcat/), queried through its [web service](https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/)). The page uses every earthquake of **magnitude 6 and above** since 1900, and every one of **magnitude 5 and above** since 1973. - **The deaths**: the Significant Earthquake Database of the US **National Centers for Environmental Information** (NCEI, part of NOAA), which lists destructive earthquakes with the number of people they killed ([NCEI](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/natural-hazards/tsunamis-earthquakes-volcanoes/earthquakes)). The USGS catalogue has no deaths. - **The map**: the boundaries of the tectonic plates, from Peter Bird's digital model ([Bird 2003](https://doi.org/10.1029/2001GC000252)) in the version of Hugo Ahlenius and Nordpil ([tectonicplates](https://github.com/fraxen/tectonicplates)), and the outlines of the countries, from [Natural Earth](https://www.naturalearthdata.com/). **The magnitude** is the size of the earthquake. Each whole number up is a tenfold increase in the ground motion that a seismograph records and 32 times more energy released ([USGS](https://www.usgs.gov/programs/earthquake-hazards/earthquake-magnitude-energy-release-and-shaking-intensity)). So a magnitude 7 earthquake releases 32 times the energy of a magnitude 6, and about a thousand times (32 × 32) that of a magnitude 5. This page writes magnitude 6 as M6, and "M6+" for magnitude 6 and above. **The depth** is how far below the surface the rock starts to break, in kilometres. The USGS calls an earthquake shallow when it is between 0 and 70 km deep, intermediate between 70 and 300 km and deep between 300 and 700 km ([USGS](https://www.usgs.gov/programs/earthquake-hazards/determining-depth-earthquake)). **The tectonic plates** are the large slabs that make up the outer shell of the Earth. They move against each other, and the earthquakes are not spread evenly: look at where the plates meet. --- ## Packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages(c("plotly", "sf", "jsonlite")) library(plotly) library(sf) library(jsonlite) ``` ::: ## The data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # only complete years: from 1 January of this year, the catalogue is incomplete last_year<-as.integer(format(Sys.Date(),"%Y"))-1 # the USGS catalogue as a table: the earthquakes between two dates, of at least a magnitude # (a query returns 20,000 earthquakes at most, so the magnitude 5 and above come in pieces) usgs<-function(from,to,magnitude) { result<-read.csv(paste0("https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/query?format=csv", "&starttime=",from,"-01-01&endtime=",to,"-01-01","&minmagnitude=", magnitude,"&orderby=time-asc&limit=20000")) return(result) } # magnitude 6 and above, since 1900 big<-usgs(1900,last_year+1,6) # magnitude 5 and above, since 1973, eight years at a time starts<-seq(1973,last_year,by=8) ends<-c(starts[-1],last_year+1) middle<-do.call(rbind,Map(function(a,b) usgs(a,b,5),starts,ends)) # the destructive earthquakes of NCEI, with deaths, since 1900, 200 to a page noaa_url<-paste0("https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/hazel/hazard-service/api/v1/earthquakes", "?minYear=1900&minDeaths=1") first_page<-fromJSON(noaa_url) deadly<-do.call(rbind,lapply(seq_len(first_page$totalPages),function(i) { fromJSON(paste0(noaa_url,"&page=",i))$items[,c("year","locationName","country","eqMagnitude", "deaths","deathsTotal","latitude","longitude")] })) # the plate boundaries (Bird 2003), and the countries (Natural Earth, 1:50 million) plates<-st_read(paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fraxen/tectonicplates/master/", "GeoJSON/PB2002_boundaries.json"),quiet=TRUE) land<-st_read(paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvkelso/natural-earth-vector/master/", "geojson/ne_50m_admin_0_countries.geojson"),quiet=TRUE) land<-land[,c("NAME_LONG","ADM0_A3","CONTINENT")] ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} red<-"#d62728" gray<-"#bdbdbd" dark_gray<-"#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes # the three depths, in order, whose neighbours were checked for colour blindness depth_colors<-c(Shallow="#d97706",Intermediate="#be123c",Deep="#5b3fb5") # one hue, from light to dark, for amounts: the map of the countries blues<-c("#eff3ff","#c6dbef","#9ecae1","#6baed6","#3182bd","#08519c","#08306b") # the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(), margin=list(t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.16,...) { note<-list(text=paste("Source:",source),xref="paper",yref="paper",x=0,y=note_y,xanchor="left", yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=11,color=dark_gray)) result<-layout(p,title=list(text=title,x=0.02,xanchor="left",y=0.97,yanchor="top"), yaxis=c(list(title=y_title),y_axis),xaxis=c(list(title=""),x_axis),margin=margin, annotations=c(annotations,list(note)),...) %>% config(displaylogo=FALSE) return(result) } legend_top<-list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.02,yanchor="bottom") # numbers in the text number<-function(x) { result<-format(round(x),big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE,trim=TRUE) return(result) } percent<-function(x,digits=0) { result<-paste0(format(round(x,digits),nsmall=digits,trim=TRUE),"%") return(result) } one<-function(x) { result<-format(round(x,1),nsmall=1,trim=TRUE) return(result) } two<-function(x) { result<-format(round(x,2),nsmall=2,trim=TRUE) return(result) } and_list<-function(x) { if(length(x)<2) { return(paste(x)) } result<-paste(paste(head(x,-1),collapse=", "),"and",tail(x,1)) return(result) } # a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one # without a trend chance<-function(x,years) { p<-cor.test(years,x,method="kendall",exact=FALSE)$p.value result<-if(p<0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100*p)) return(result) } # the distance in kilometres between two points (longitude and latitude in degrees) distance_km<-function(lon1,lat1,lon2,lat2) { r<-pi/180 h<-sin((lat2-lat1)*r/2)^2+cos(lat1*r)*cos(lat2*r)*sin((lon2-lon1)*r/2)^2 result<-12742*asin(sqrt(h)) return(result) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # only earthquakes: the catalogue also holds explosions, and more all_types<-table(c(big$type,middle$type)) n_blasts<-sum(all_types[names(all_types)=="nuclear explosion"]) n_other<-sum(all_types[!names(all_types)%in%c("earthquake","nuclear explosion")]) quakes<-function(x) { x<-x[x$type=="earthquake",] x$year<-as.integer(substr(x$time,1,4)) return(x) } n_before<-nrow(big)+nrow(middle) big<-quakes(big) middle<-quakes(middle) magnitude_types<-sort(table(middle$magType),decreasing=TRUE) # the depth classes of the USGS depth_class<-function(depth) { result<-cut(depth,c(-Inf,70,300,Inf),labels=names(depth_colors),right=FALSE) return(result) } middle$depth_class<-depth_class(middle$depth) big$depth_class<-depth_class(big$depth) # depths that a location program sets when the data do not fix the depth (USGS: 10 and 33 km) fixed_depth<-mean(middle$depth%in%c(10,33)) other_depth<-max(table(middle$depth[!middle$depth%in%c(10,33)]))/nrow(middle) above_sea<-sum(middle$depth<0) # each earthquake of magnitude 5 and above: the country it is in; or the nearest country, if the # sea is less than 200 km wide between the two; or nowhere. Planar geometry on longitude and # latitude is accurate enough to find the nearest country; the distance itself is then worked out # on the globe. sf_use_s2(FALSE) points<-st_as_sf(middle[,c("id","longitude","latitude")],coords=c("longitude","latitude"),crs=4326) inside<-st_intersects(points,land) on_land<-lengths(inside)>0 nearest<-st_nearest_feature(points[!on_land,],land) lines<-st_nearest_points(points[!on_land,],land[nearest,],pairwise=TRUE) ends_xy<-st_coordinates(st_cast(lines,"POINT")) from_xy<-ends_xy[seq(1,nrow(ends_xy),by=2),] to_xy<-ends_xy[seq(2,nrow(ends_xy),by=2),] offshore_km<-distance_km(from_xy[,1],from_xy[,2],to_xy[,1],to_xy[,2]) middle$place_index<-NA_integer_ middle$place_index[on_land]<-vapply(inside[on_land],`[`,1L,1L) reach<-200 middle$place_index[!on_land][offshore_km<=reach]<-nearest[offshore_km<=reach] land$NAME_LONG[land$NAME_LONG=="Russian Federation"]<-"Russia" land$NAME_LONG[land$NAME_LONG=="South Georgia and the Islands"]<-"South Georgia" middle$country<-land$NAME_LONG[middle$place_index] middle$code<-land$ADM0_A3[middle$place_index] middle$continent<-land$CONTINENT[middle$place_index] # each earthquake of magnitude 6 and above since 1973: its distance from the nearest plate boundary big_now<-big[big$year>=1973,] points_now<-st_as_sf(big_now[,c("id","longitude","latitude")],coords=c("longitude","latitude"), crs=4326) near_boundary<-st_nearest_feature(points_now,plates) lines_now<-st_nearest_points(points_now,plates[near_boundary,],pairwise=TRUE) xy_now<-st_coordinates(st_cast(lines_now,"POINT")) from_now<-xy_now[seq(1,nrow(xy_now),by=2),] to_now<-xy_now[seq(2,nrow(xy_now),by=2),] big_now$boundary_km<-distance_km(from_now[,1],from_now[,2],to_now[,1],to_now[,2]) # the same distance for points spread evenly over the globe: how much of the world is near a # boundary set.seed(2026) n_random<-4000 random_points<-st_as_sf(data.frame(lon=runif(n_random,-180,180), lat=asin(runif(n_random,-1,1))*180/pi), coords=c("lon","lat"),crs=4326) near_random<-st_nearest_feature(random_points,plates) lines_random<-st_cast(st_nearest_points(random_points,plates[near_random,],pairwise=TRUE),"POINT") xy_random<-st_coordinates(lines_random) from_random<-xy_random[seq(1,nrow(xy_random),by=2),] to_random<-xy_random[seq(2,nrow(xy_random),by=2),] random_km<-distance_km(from_random[,1],from_random[,2],to_random[,1],to_random[,2]) sf_use_s2(TRUE) # the deaths: the NCEI total where it has one deadly$deaths_all<-ifelse(is.na(deadly$deathsTotal),deadly$deaths,deadly$deathsTotal) deadly<-deadly[!is.na(deadly$deaths_all)&deadly$year<=last_year,] deadly$name<-ifelse(deadly$country=="USA","United States", tools::toTitleCase(tolower(deadly$country))) # the place as NCEI writes it, in words: the parts between colons, without compass points place_text<-function(x) { parts<-strsplit(tolower(x),"\\s*:\\s*") result<-vapply(parts,function(p) { p<-trimws(p) paste(tools::toTitleCase(p[!p%in%c("n","s","e","w","ne","nw","se","sw","")]),collapse=", ") },"") return(result) } deadly$place<-place_text(deadly$locationName) ``` ::: **Only earthquakes.** The catalogue also holds explosions, mine collapses and landslides. Of the 102,788 events that the two downloads found, 494 were nuclear explosions and 69 were other things (an explosion, a rock burst, a volcanic eruption and so on). The page uses the other 102,225, labelled earthquakes. 14,358 of them are magnitude 6 and above since 1900 and 87,867 magnitude 5 and above since 1973, and the second group includes most of the first from 1973 on. **Only whole years.** The page stops at the end of 2025, so that every year counts in full. **Many magnitudes.** The catalogue gives each earthquake the magnitude that its source chose, of several kinds: from 1973 on, 47% of the magnitude 5 and above are of the kind called mb, and the others are of kinds such as Mw (the moment magnitude, the one that scientists prefer for large earthquakes). Section 5 shows what that means for counting earthquakes over the years. **Which country?** The catalogue's place is a piece of text, not a country code, so each earthquake of magnitude 5 and above is placed on the map of the countries. Only 20% fall inside a country: the rest happen under the sea. An earthquake at sea is given to the nearest country when it is within 200 km of its coast (56% of all of them); the other 24%, in the open sea, belong to no country. Countries are those of Natural Earth, which counts overseas territories (Puerto Rico, Guam) as places of their own, and a country's earthquakes are the ones under it and near it. **The depth is the least certain number.** It is the least constrained of all the parameters of an earthquake, says the USGS, and where the data do not fix it, the location program sets a default, often 10 or 33 km ([ComCat](https://earthquake.usgs.gov/data/comcat/data-eventterms.php)). 40% of the magnitude 5 and above have exactly 10 or 33 km (the next most common depth has 3%), so the depths on this page are good for classes (shallow, intermediate, deep) and not for the exact kilometre. 27 of them are negative, which means above the reference level that the source used. --- ## 1. Where in the world do the earthquakes strike? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n_big<-nrow(big_now) within<-function(km) { result<-percent(100*mean(big_now$boundary_km<=km)) return(result) } world_within<-function(km) { result<-percent(100*mean(random_km<=km)) return(result) } # the earthquakes of each country, the most first (a key of the three columns keeps a missing code) on_land<-middle[!is.na(middle$country),] keys<-paste(on_land$country,on_land$code,on_land$continent,sep="|") places<-do.call(rbind,lapply(split(on_land,keys),function(x) { data.frame(country=x$country[1], code=x$code[1], continent=x$continent[1], n=nrow(x), strong=sum(x$mag>=6)) })) places<-places[order(-places$n,places$country,method="radix"),] rownames(places)<-NULL n_years<-last_year-1973+1 n_places<-nrow(places) top<-head(places,15) sea_share<-100*mean(is.na(middle$country)) place_of<-function(name,column) { result<-places[[column]][places$country==name] return(result) } rank_of<-function(name) { result<-match(name,places$country) return(result) } # Europe: the continent of Natural Earth, without Russia (most of its earthquakes are in Kamchatka # and the Kuril Islands, in the east) and with Turkey, which Natural Earth puts in Asia, counted # on its own europe<-head(places[which(places$continent=="Europe"&places$country!="Russia"),],4) ``` ::: **Along narrow belts, and mostly under the sea.** The 7,327 earthquakes of magnitude 6 and above from 1973 to 2025 do not fall at random: 65% of them are within 100 km of a plate boundary and 92% within 300 km. Of the surface of the globe, only 10% is within 100 km of a boundary and 24% within 300 km (worked out for 4,000 points spread evenly over the globe). Where plates meet, one slides under the other, or they grind side by side, and the rock breaks. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the plate boundaries as one line with gaps coords<-as.data.frame(st_coordinates(plates)) gaps<-do.call(rbind,lapply(split(coords[,c("X","Y")],coords$L1),function(x) { rbind(x,data.frame(X=NA,Y=NA)) })) shown<-big_now shown$text<-paste0("M",format(shown$mag,nsmall=1),", ",shown$year,", ",round(shown$depth), " km deep") p<-plot_ly() %>% add_trace(type="scattergeo",mode="lines",lon=round(gaps$X,2),lat=round(gaps$Y,2), line=list(color=dark_gray,width=0.8),name="Plate boundaries",hoverinfo="skip") depth_ranges<-c(Shallow="under 70 km",Intermediate="70–300 km",Deep="300 km or more") for(k in names(depth_colors)) { x<-shown[shown$depth_class==k,] p<-add_trace(p,type="scattergeo",mode="markers",lon=x$longitude,lat=x$latitude,text=x$text, hoverinfo="text",name=paste0(k," (",depth_ranges[[k]],")"), marker=list(color=depth_colors[[k]],size=4.5,opacity=0.75,line=list(width=0))) } p %>% chart(paste0("Earthquakes of magnitude 6 and above, 1973–",last_year), paste0("USGS ComCat; plate boundaries: Bird (2003), ", "via Ahlenius/Nordpil; countries: Natural Earth."), geo=list(showframe=FALSE,showcoastlines=TRUE,coastlinecolor="#cccccc",showland=TRUE, landcolor="#f0f0f0",projection=list(type="natural earth"), lataxis=list(range=c(-65,85))), legend=list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.0,yanchor="bottom"),margin=list(t=80,b=40,l=0,r=0), note_y=-0.02) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **Indonesia leads, then Papua New Guinea and Japan.** Counting every earthquake of magnitude 5 and above from 1973 to 2025 under a country or within 200 km of its coast, Indonesia had 11,920, Papua New Guinea 5,488 and Japan 5,093: 224.9, 103.5 and 96.1 a year. 24% of all the earthquakes of this size were farther than 200 km from any country. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bars<-top[order(top$n),] bars$country<-factor(bars$country,levels=bars$country) plot_ly(bars,x=~n,y=~country,type="bar",orientation="h", marker=list(color=ifelse(bars$strong==max(bars$strong),red,gray)),text=~number(n), textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE, hovertemplate=paste0("%{y}: %{x} earthquakes, of which %{customdata} of magnitude ", "6 and above"), customdata=~strong,showlegend=FALSE) %>% chart(paste0("Most earthquakes of magnitude 5+, ",1973,"–",last_year), "USGS ComCat; countries: Natural Earth. Red: the most of magnitude 6 and above.", x_axis=list(range=c(0,1.25*max(bars$n)),showgrid=FALSE),margin=list(l=160,t=70,b=60,r=20), note_y=-0.1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} on_map<-places[places$code%in%land$ADM0_A3,] classes<-c(1,10,50,100,500,1000,Inf) class_names<-c("1–9","10–49","50–99","100–499","500–999","1,000+") on_map$class<-as.integer(cut(on_map$n,classes,right=FALSE)) steps<-do.call(c,lapply(seq_along(class_names),function(i) { list(list((i-1)/6,blues[i+1]),list(i/6,blues[i+1])) })) plot_ly(on_map,type="choropleth",locations=~code,z=~class,zmin=0.5,zmax=6.5,colorscale=steps, marker=list(line=list(color="white",width=0.3)), text=~paste0(country,": ",number(n)," earthquakes of magnitude 5+
",strong, " of magnitude 6+"), hoverinfo="text", colorbar=list(title=list(text="Earthquakes of magnitude 5+",side="top"),orientation="h", x=0.5,xanchor="center",y=-0.02,yanchor="top",tickvals=1:6, ticktext=class_names,len=0.95,thickness=14,tickangle=0, tickfont=list(size=10))) %>% chart(paste0("Earthquakes of magnitude 5+ by country, ",1973,"–",last_year), paste0("USGS ComCat; countries: Natural Earth. ", "Under the country or within 200 km of its coast. Grey: none."), geo=list(showframe=FALSE,showcoastlines=FALSE,showland=TRUE,landcolor="#e8e8e8", projection=list(type="natural earth"),lataxis=list(range=c(-57,85))), margin=list(t=50,b=130,l=0,r=0),note_y=-0.27) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} turkey<-"Turkey" greece<-"Greece" europe_list<-paste0(europe$country," (",number(europe$n),")") greece_strong<-place_of(greece,"strong") ``` ::: **In Europe, Greece comes first.** In 172 countries and territories with at least one earthquake of magnitude 5 and above, Greece is number 22: 552 earthquakes since 1973, 58 of magnitude 6 and above, 10.4 a year. Without Russia, the four European countries with the most are Greece (552), Iceland (135), Italy (133) and Norway (92). Turkey, which Natural Earth places in Asia, is number 29 with 356. --- ## 2. How often, and how strong? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} modern<-1990 # the magnitude classes: the lower end and the name classes_m<-list("5–5.9"=c(5,6),"6–6.9"=c(6,7),"7–7.9"=c(7,8),"8 and above"=c(8,11)) per_year<-sapply(classes_m,function(r) { sum(middle$mag>=r[1]&middle$mag=modern)/(last_year-modern+1) }) big_per_year<-sapply(classes_m[3:4],function(r) { sum(big$mag>=r[1]&big$mag=8) strongest<-big[which(big$mag>=8),] n8_years<-aggregate(n~year,data.frame(year=strongest$year,n=1L),sum) ``` ::: **About 1,500 a year of magnitude 5 and 0.9 of magnitude 8.** From 1990 to 2025, the catalogue records on average 1,547 earthquakes of magnitude 5 to 5.9 a year, 135 of magnitude 6 to 6.9, 14 of magnitude 7 to 7.9 and 0.9 of magnitude 8 and above. Each step up is rarer: 11.5 times, 9.6 times and 14.9 times. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knitr::kable(data.frame(magnitude=names(per_year), year=ifelse(per_year>=10,number(per_year),one(per_year)), month=one(per_year/12), week=two(per_year/52)), col.names=c("Magnitude","A year","A month","A week"),align="lrrr",row.names=FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Magnitude | A year| A month| A week| |:-----------|------:|-------:|------:| |5–5.9 | 1,547| 128.9| 29.75| |6–6.9 | 135| 11.3| 2.60| |7–7.9 | 14| 1.2| 0.27| |8 and above | 0.9| 0.1| 0.02| ::: ::: **The largest.** 100 earthquakes of magnitude 8 and above since 1900, 0.8 a year; the ten largest are in the table, with the magnitude that the catalogue gives them. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knitr::kable(data.frame(place=largest$place_short, year=substr(largest$time,1,4), magnitude=one(largest$mag), depth=round(largest$depth)), col.names=c("Where (USGS)","Year","Magnitude","Depth, km"),align="llrr", row.names=FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Where (USGS) |Year | Magnitude| Depth, km| |:--------------------------------------------------------------|:----|---------:|---------:| |1960 Great Chilean Earthquake (Valdivia Earthquake) |1960 | 9.5| 25| |The 1964 Prince William Sound, Alaska Earthquake |1964 | 9.2| 25| |2004 Sumatra - Andaman Islands Earthquake |2004 | 9.1| 30| |2011 Great Tohoku Earthquake, Japan |2011 | 9.1| 29| |Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, Russia |1952 | 9.0| 22| |1906 Ecuador-Colombia Earthquake |1906 | 8.8| 20| |2010 Maule, Chile Earthquake |2010 | 8.8| 23| |2025 Kamchatka Peninsula, Russia Earthquake |2025 | 8.8| 35| |1965 Western Aleutian Islands (Hawadax/Rat Islands) Earthquake |1965 | 8.7| 30| |The 1946 Unimak Island, Alaska Earthquake |1946 | 8.6| 15| ::: ::: --- ## 3. How deep are they? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} share_of<-function(x,k) { result<-100*mean(x$depth_class==k) return(result) } by_size<-list("5–5.9"=middle[middle$mag<6,],"6–6.9"=middle[middle$mag>=6&middle$mag<7,], "7 and above"=middle[middle$mag>=7,]) shares<-do.call(rbind,lapply(names(by_size),function(s) { data.frame(size=s, k=names(depth_colors), share=sapply(names(depth_colors),function(k) share_of(by_size[[s]],k))) })) deep<-middle[middle$depth_class=="Deep",] deep_places<-sort(table(deep$country),decreasing=TRUE) deepest<-middle[which.max(middle$depth),] deep_share_n<-sum(deep$mag>=7) ``` ::: **Nearly all of them are shallow.** 79% of the earthquakes of magnitude 5 and above since 1973 began less than 70 km down, 16% between 70 and 300 km and 4.8% below 300 km. Among those of magnitude 7 and above, 77% were shallow. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shares$size<-factor(shares$size,levels=rev(names(by_size))) shares$k<-factor(shares$k,levels=names(depth_colors)) p<-plot_ly() for(k in names(depth_colors)) { x<-shares[shares$k==k,] p<-add_bars(p,x=x$share,y=x$size,name=k,orientation="h", marker=list(color=depth_colors[[k]],line=list(color="white",width=1.5)), text=ifelse(x$share>=10,percent(x$share),""),textposition="inside", insidetextanchor="middle",textfont=list(color="white"), hovertemplate=paste0("Magnitude %{y}: %{x:.1f}% ",tolower(k),"")) } p %>% chart("How deep, % of the earthquakes of each size", paste0("USGS ComCat, 1973 on. Shallow: under 70 km; ", "intermediate: 70–300 km; deep: 300 km or more."), x_axis=list(range=c(0,100),ticksuffix="%",showgrid=FALSE),y_axis=list(title="Magnitude"), barmode="stack",legend=c(legend_top,list(traceorder="normal")), uniformtext=list(minsize=10,mode="hide"),margin=list(l=110,t=90,b=70,r=10),note_y=-0.22) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **The deep ones are in a few places.** 4,201 earthquakes of magnitude 5 and above were deep, 61 of them of magnitude 7 and above. The countries (or the coasts) with the most were Fiji (1,694), Indonesia (430) and Russia (122); 32% were in the open sea. The deepest of all, of magnitude 5.5, was 700 km down: 281 km SE of Levuka, Fiji, in 1985. --- ## 4. Which were the deadliest? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} worst<-head(deadly[order(-deadly$deaths_all),],10) worst_n<-nrow(deadly) total_deaths<-sum(deadly$deaths_all) # the deaths of each country, the most first country_groups<-split(deadly,addNA(factor(deadly$name),ifany=TRUE)) deaths_by_country<-do.call(rbind,lapply(country_groups,function(x) { data.frame(name=x$name[1],deaths=sum(x$deaths_all),n=nrow(x)) })) deaths_by_country<-deaths_by_country[order(-deaths_by_country$deaths,deaths_by_country$name, method="radix"),] rownames(deaths_by_country)<-NULL top10_share<-100*sum(worst$deaths_all)/total_deaths top_c<-head(deaths_by_country,10) since<-min(deadly$year) n_over_10k<-sum(deadly$deaths_all>=10000) n_below_7<-mean(deadly$eqMagnitude[!is.na(deadly$eqMagnitude)]<7) # the ten largest earthquakes of section 2: the deaths of the earthquake of the same year within # 500 km largest_deaths<-sapply(seq_len(nrow(largest)),function(i) { near<-deadly$year==as.integer(substr(largest$time[i],1,4))& distance_km(largest$longitude[i],largest$latitude[i],deadly$longitude,deadly$latitude)<=500 near[is.na(near)]<-FALSE if(any(near)) max(deadly$deaths_all[near]) else 0 }) # the events where the NCEI total differs from its deaths, and the largest example all_rows<-deadly[!is.na(deadly$deaths)&!is.na(deadly$deathsTotal)&deadly$deathsTotal>deadly$deaths,] example<-all_rows[which.max(all_rows$deathsTotal-all_rows$deaths),] ``` ::: **A few earthquakes account for most of the deaths.** NCEI lists 1,595 earthquakes since 1900 with a recorded number of deaths, 2,531,015 in all. The ten deadliest killed 1,548,214 of them, 61%, and 37 killed 10,000 or more. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knitr::kable(data.frame(year=worst$year, place=worst$place, magnitude=ifelse(is.na(worst$eqMagnitude),"",one(worst$eqMagnitude)), deaths=number(worst$deaths_all)), col.names=c("Year","Where (NCEI)","Magnitude","Deaths"),align="llrr",row.names=FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Year |Where (NCEI) | Magnitude| Deaths| |:----|:-----------------------------------------------|---------:|-------:| |2010 |Haiti, Port-Au-Prince | 7.0| 316,000| |1976 |China, Tangshan | 7.5| 242,769| |1920 |China, Gansu Province, Shanxi Province | 8.3| 235,502| |2004 |Indonesia, Sumatra, Aceh, Off West Coast | 9.1| 227,899| |1948 |Turkmenistan, Ashkhabad | 7.2| 110,000| |1923 |Japan, Tokyo, Yokohama | 7.9| 105,385| |2008 |China, Sichuan Province | 7.9| 87,652| |1908 |Italy, Messina, Sicily, Calabria | 7.0| 80,000| |2005 |Pakistan, Muzaffarabad, Uri, Anantnag, Baramula | 7.6| 76,213| |1970 |Peru, Northern, Pisco, Chiclayo | 7.9| 66,794| ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bars<-top_c[order(top_c$deaths),] bars$name<-factor(bars$name,levels=bars$name) plot_ly(bars,x=~deaths,y=~name,type="bar",orientation="h", marker=list(color=ifelse(bars$deaths==max(bars$deaths),red,gray)),text=~number(deaths), textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE, hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x:,.0f} deaths in %{customdata} earthquakes", customdata=~n,showlegend=FALSE) %>% chart(paste0("Deaths in earthquakes since ",since,", 10 countries"), "NCEI Significant Earthquake Database. Deaths as recorded, in the country that NCEI names.", x_axis=list(range=c(0,1.3*max(bars$deaths)),showgrid=FALSE), margin=list(l=120,t=70,b=60,r=20),note_y=-0.1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **Not the strongest earthquakes.** The ten deadliest were of magnitude 7.0 to 9.1. Of the ten largest earthquakes of section 2, 4 killed 1,000 or more people (by NCEI's list), and 4 have no deaths in it. Of the 1,546 earthquakes in NCEI's list with a magnitude, 74% were below magnitude 7. How many die depends on where the earthquake strikes, who lives there and how they build, as well as on the magnitude, and the data here cannot separate those. **Which deaths?** NCEI gives two figures: the deaths and a total. They differ for 42 earthquakes since 1900, and the largest difference is the 2004 earthquake (Indonesia, Sumatra, Aceh, Off West Coast): 1,001 deaths and 227,899 in total, with a tsunami linked to it in the database. The page uses the total where there is one. --- ## 5. Are there more of them than there used to be? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} years_big<-1900:last_year count_by_year<-function(x,lo,years) { tab<-table(factor(x$year[x$mag>=lo],levels=years)) result<-data.frame(year=years,n=as.integer(tab)) return(result) } m7<-count_by_year(big,7,1900:last_year) m6<-count_by_year(big,6,1900:last_year) m6_modern<-m6[m6$year>=1973,] m5<-count_by_year(middle,5,1973:last_year) # the year after which the yearly counts of magnitude 6 and above are on another level (the split # of the years that leaves the least spread within the two parts) split_cost<-sapply(1976:(last_year-3),function(y) { a<-m6_modern$n[m6_modern$year=y] sum((a-mean(a))^2)+sum((b-mean(b))^2) }) step_year<-(1976:(last_year-3))[which.min(split_cost)] before_step<-mean(m6_modern$n[m6_modern$year=step_year]) m6_first<-mean(m6$n[m6$year<=1904]) m6_next<-mean(m6$n[m6$year%in%1905:1914]) m7_first<-mean(m7$n[m7$year<=1904]) m7_all<-mean(m7$n) m7_periods<-c(early=mean(m7$n[m7$year<=1949]),middle=mean(m7$n[m7$year%in%1950:1989]), late=mean(m7$n[m7$year>=1990])) tests<-data.frame(what=c("M7+","M7+","M6+","M5+"), from=c(1900,modern,step_year,step_year), chance=c(chance(m7$n,m7$year), chance(m7$n[m7$year>=modern],m7$year[m7$year>=modern]), chance(m6$n[m6$year>=step_year],m6$year[m6$year>=step_year]), chance(m5$n[m5$year>=step_year],m5$year[m5$year>=step_year])), stringsAsFactors=FALSE) means_of<-function(x,from,to) { result<-mean(x$n[x$year>=from&x$year<=to]) return(result) } # one big earthquake brings its aftershocks: the Tohoku earthquake of 2011 and the following year in_2011<-big[big$year==2011,] tohoku<-in_2011[which.max(in_2011$mag),] tohoku_time<-as.POSIXct(tohoku$time,format="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S",tz="UTC") middle_time<-as.POSIXct(middle$time,format="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S",tz="UTC") after<-middle_time>tohoku_time&middle_time<=tohoku_time+365*86400& distance_km(tohoku$longitude,tohoku$latitude,middle$longitude,middle$latitude)<=500 after_n<-sum(after) year_2011<-m5$n[m5$year==2011] peak_year<-m5$year[which.max(m5$n)] ``` ::: **No clear trend in the big ones; the smaller ones are counted in steps.** Earthquakes of magnitude 7 and above are the only ones that the catalogue seems to record in full since 1900 (see below). They averaged 12.4 a year from 1900 to 1949, 11.1 from 1950 to 1989 and 15.0 from 1990 to 2025: not a steady rise. From 1990 on, a rank test finds no trend in them (the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend is 64 in 100). Over all the years from 1900 the test leans slightly upwards (3 in 100), because of the dip in the middle of the century; the page does not take that for a lasting rise, since magnitudes were worked out differently in each period. For the smaller earthquakes the catalogue is the problem, not the Earth. From 1900 to 1904 it holds 15.4 earthquakes of magnitude 6 and above a year, and from 1905 to 1914 55.8; for magnitude 7 and above the same years give 12.0 and 15.7, so only the strongest were recorded in those years. Even from 1973 the counts of magnitude 6 and above are not on one level: they average 93.1 a year before 1983 and 148.7 from 1983 on, a step of 60%. The page does not know why the catalogue steps there. So the tests for magnitude 6 and above and for 5 and above start in 1983, where the rank test finds no clear trend either (the last column): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knitr::kable(data.frame(what=c("Magnitude 7 and above","Magnitude 7 and above", "Magnitude 6 and above","Magnitude 5 and above"), from=paste0(tests$from,"–",last_year), average=c(one(means_of(m7,1900,last_year)), one(means_of(m7,modern,last_year)), one(means_of(m6,step_year,last_year)), number(means_of(m5,step_year,last_year))), chance=tests$chance), col.names=c("","Years","A year, on average","By chance, in 100"),align="llrr", row.names=FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | |Years | A year, on average| By chance, in 100| |:---------------------|:---------|------------------:|-----------------:| |Magnitude 7 and above |1900–2025 | 12.8| 3| |Magnitude 7 and above |1990–2025 | 15.0| 64| |Magnitude 6 and above |1983–2025 | 148.7| 46| |Magnitude 5 and above |1983–2025 | 1,692| 18| ::: ::: **Aftershocks can make a year.** A large earthquake is followed by many smaller ones, and a simple count does not tell them from new earthquakes. After the Tohoku earthquake in Japan (magnitude 9.1, 2011-03-11), 779 earthquakes of magnitude 5 and above happened within 500 km in the following year, 29% of the 2,701 of the whole of 2011, and 779 is 46% of the average year since 1983. The year with the most of magnitude 5 and above was 2011, with 2,701. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # one panel: the earthquakes counted each year count_panel<-function(x,title) { result<-plot_ly(x,x=~year,y=~n,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers",name=title, line=list(color=dark_gray,width=1),marker=list(color=dark_gray,size=4), hovertemplate=paste0("%{x}: %{y}",title,"")) return(result) } titles<-c("Magnitude 7 and above, since 1900", paste0("Magnitude 6 and above, since 1973; red: the average before and from ",step_year), "Magnitude 5 and above, since 1973") middle_panel<-count_panel(m6_modern,titles[2]) %>% add_segments(x=c(1973-0.4,step_year-0.5),xend=c(step_year-0.5,last_year+0.4), y=c(before_step,after_step),yend=c(before_step,after_step), line=list(color=red,width=3),name="Average", hovertemplate="Average: %{y:.1f} a year") p<-subplot(count_panel(m7,titles[1]),middle_panel,count_panel(m5,titles[3]),nrows=3,margin=0.07) # the title of each panel, above it domains<-plotly_build(p)$x$layout[c("yaxis","yaxis2","yaxis3")] panel_titles<-lapply(1:3,function(k) { list(text=paste0("",titles[k],""),x=0,xref="paper",y=domains[[k]]$domain[2],yref="paper", xanchor="left",yanchor="bottom",showarrow=FALSE) }) p %>% chart("Earthquakes counted each year","USGS ComCat",y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero"), annotations=panel_titles,showlegend=FALSE,margin=list(t=80,b=70),note_y=-0.08, yaxis2=list(rangemode="tozero"),yaxis3=list(rangemode="tozero")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: --- ## So, what does it mean? 1. **Earthquakes come in belts.** 65% of the 7,327 of magnitude 6 and above since 1973 struck within 100 km of a plate boundary, which is near only 10% of the surface of the globe. 24% of those of magnitude 5 and above were farther than 200 km from any country. 2. **Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and Japan have the most.** Greece is number 22 among 172 countries and territories, and the first in Europe without Russia. 3. **There are about 0.9 earthquakes of magnitude 8 a year and about 14 of magnitude 7**, and each step down in magnitude is several times as common. 4. **Nearly all are shallow**, 79% of those of magnitude 5 and above. The deaths come in a few events: the ten deadliest earthquakes killed 61% of the 2,531,015 recorded since 1900. 5. **There is no clear sign of more earthquakes in this catalogue.** From 1990 on there is no trend in those of magnitude 7 and above; the smaller ones are counted in steps, and the page does not claim a trend for them. **What this does not show.** The catalogue is of the earthquakes that instruments record, and the earlier years of it are patchy for all but the strongest. The magnitude is of several kinds, and the depth is uncertain. The countries come from the places of the earthquakes, not from where the shaking was felt. The deaths are those NCEI recorded for its significant earthquakes: some counts are estimates, and the tsunamis that follow some earthquakes are not told apart here. And earthquakes of the same size do not do the same harm.
